name: solidcraft-agent-tools
description: "Use when running SolidCraft to see a change working, driving it through the control channel or CLI, or adding or changing an MCP tool, control method or bundled agent skill."
---

# Running the app, the control channel and MCP tools

## Run it and look at it
- `cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample --control PORT` starts the sample design with the control channel. Pick a free port. With no display, run it under `Xvfb :99` with `DISPLAY=:99`.
- Talk JSON lines to `127.0.0.1:PORT` (`docs/control-protocol.md`). The first request on a connection carries the launch token as `"token"`: read it from `~/.local/share/solidcraft/control/PORT.token`, or start the app with `SOLIDCRAFT_CONTROL_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)` and send that. Never paste the token into a PR or issue.
  - `{"id":1,"method":"engine.execute","params":{"command":"solid.extrude","params":{"distance":20}}}`
  - `{"id":2,"method":"ui.start","params":{"command":"sketch.create"}}`, then `ui.click {x, y}`
  - `{"id":3,"method":"ui.screenshot","params":{"path":"/tmp/shot.png"}}`, then read the PNG
- For UI work, look at the result. Without a window use `ui.render` or `solidcraft-cli snapshot`.
- Headless: `solidcraft-cli run script.json --out part.step`, `solidcraft-cli eval design.sc`, `solidcraft-cli snapshot script.json --out shot.png`, `solidcraft-cli commands`.
- Build with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<repo>/target`.

## MCP tools
The server is `solidcraft-cli mcp` (`crates/mcp/src/`, `docs/mcp.md`). Tools are defined in `crates/mcp/src/tools.rs`; keep `docs/mcp.md` in step, and keep tool annotations (read-only, destructive) honest.
- Anything the user can do is a command; add a command, not a new tool, unless the tool is about the session itself (open, save, screenshot, batch).
- Files: tools reach only the allowed folders (the design's folder, the recovery folder, the scratch folder, `--allow-path`). Do not widen this casually; paths are resolved before comparing, so `..` and links leaving the allowed set are refused, and on Windows UNC and device paths are refused.
- Replies stay small: `verbose: false`, no unfiltered command catalogue or topology dumps.
- The control channel is a local-only interface with a token. A new method needs an entry in `docs/control-protocol.md`; long work follows `skills/solidcraft-performance/SKILL.md`.

## Bundled agent skills
The modelling skills (`skills/solidcraft-modeling`, `-editing`, `-checking`, `-mechanisms`) are built into the MCP server for its `skill_reference` tool (`crates/mcp/src/skill_reference.rs`). The contributor skills are not.
- When a command, parameter name or behaviour those skills describe changes, update them in the same PR. `skills_name_only_real_tools_and_commands` in `crates/mcp/src/tests.rs` fails when a skill names a tool or command that is gone.
- Adding a bundled file means adding it to `skill_reference.rs` and to that test.
- `skills/README.md` explains the layout and the other tests; `cargo xtask skills` checks that AGENTS.md and every SKILL.md cite real paths, commands and skills.

---
name: solidcraft-checking
description: Use alongside solidcraft-modeling and solidcraft-editing whenever you build, change or port a SolidCraft design. Checks for errors SolidCraft does not report (parameter ranges, every allowed value, exact STEP comparison), regression tests, designs kept in git, porting from build123d, CadQuery, OpenSCAD or STEP.
---

# SolidCraft checking

`solidcraft-modeling` and `solidcraft-editing` cover the commands, plane axes, ids, edge picks and the MCP workflow: load the one that fits first. This skill adds checks for errors SolidCraft does not report, and the work around a design kept in a repo.

`$SKILL` below is the folder this file is in (`~/.claude/skills/solidcraft-checking` for a user install). Checked against SolidCraft 0.21.0. `scripts/tests/test_facts.py` checks every trap and convention below, and the facts behind the corrections in `solidcraft-modeling`. After a SolidCraft upgrade, run the tests and fix the text where they fail:
`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 uv run --no-project --with pytest --with build123d pytest -p no:cacheprovider $SKILL/scripts/tests`

## Scripts

An MCP `batch` and a command script (`{"commands": [...]}`, run by `solidcraft-cli run`) take the same command list. Build with a script when the design goes into a repo or must be rebuilt later: a script rebuilds the design from scratch on every run. Subagents share the session's one MCP design, so agents that run in parallel use `solidcraft-cli` only.

In `$SKILL/scripts/`:
- `python3 $SKILL/scripts/run.py script.json [--in <design>] [--save <name>.json]` runs a script and prints `FAIL`, a `WARN` line per feature warning, a `SKETCH` line per sketch above dof 0 and a `BODY` line per body, for the end state and for each `document.inspect` inside the script.
- `scb.py` gives a generator a `Script` with sketch helpers that come out at dof 0 (`hexagon`, `circle`, `rounded_rectangle`, `place`) and `cmd` for any other command. It rejects repeated sketch, feature and body names. Import it with `sys.path.insert(0, "<$SKILL>/scripts")`.
- `uv run --no-project --with build123d python $SKILL/scripts/compare_step.py actual.step expected.step` gives the exact volume of the difference between two STEP files and where it sits. It and the tests run OpenCASCADE through build123d as a separate tool, the way `tools/freecad-oracle` runs FreeCAD: SolidCraft does not use, link, vendor or ship any of it.
- `solidcraft-cli snapshot <design or script> --out shot.png --view iso` renders a PNG to look at.

## Steps to add

1. **Parameters and features.** Each parameter comment states the allowed range ("whole number, 4 or more"): the user reads it in the Parameters table, and SolidCraft enforces no range. Derive sizes from measured values, so that a count parameter changes how many features there are, not how big they are. An expression that more than one sketch or feature uses becomes a named parameter. Add the derived numbers the user needs (parts to print) and mark the driving parameters favourite (`parameters.favorite`). Give each thing the user thinks of (a port, a row of standoffs) its own feature, named after it, so it can be found and changed on its own. Choose the origin so that no sketch dimension reaches 0 for any allowed value (trap 1).
2. **Every sketch at dof 0.** A sketch with dof left can solve to a different shape after a parameter change, without an error. `run.py` lists them.
3. **Every allowed value.** One script of `parameters.change` commands walks each driving parameter to both ends of its range, one change after another, and back to the default, as edits in the app do: trap 1 fails only on the change after the one that reaches 0. Put a `document.inspect {measure: true}` after each end of a range and run the walk with `run.py walk.json --in <design>`. Every state must be clean: no `FAIL`, no `SKETCH`, and `BODY` volumes and centres of mass that match the values you compute for that state. A boolean retry can leave the geometry wrong with only a `WARN` line, and the volume shows it (trap 4); a mirrored sketch (trap 1) keeps the volume and moves the centre of mass.
4. **Exact check** when a port has a reference, or a volume gap leaves doubt: export STEP (`file.export {path, bodies}`) and run `compare_step.py`. Before porting, in SolidCraft's own chat or any MCP client, call `skill_reference {"skill":"solidcraft-checking","file":"reference/porting.md"}`. Elsewhere, read `$SKILL/reference/porting.md`.
5. **Kept in a repo.** Save as `<name>.json` with `run.py build.json --save <name>.json`: a `.json` design stays plain JSON when it is saved again, so git diffs stay readable. Saving over a file leaves `<name>.json.bak`, so ignore `*.bak`. From then on the design file is the source, and changes go into it with `--in <design> --save <design>`. Copy `$SKILL/templates/test_design.py` next to the design, fill in its cases, set its tolerance as its comment says, and run it until it passes. Expected values come from an exact reference when porting, from hand calculation for simple shapes, or from a build the user has reviewed. After a change, update frozen values only where the change is meant to change them.

## Traps

1. **Zero dimension.** A sketch dimension driven to 0 loses its side: the point it measures has no direction left, so the solver may leave it anywhere on the axis. On the next parameter change it either fails with `its constraints would conflict` (a point placed by dimensions from the origin) or, with no error, moves it: a slot that other constraints also held slides to the origin when the distance reaches 0 and, the solver taking the shortest step that fits, keeps the side it was drawn on when the value comes back. Check every distance expression against the whole allowed range of each parameter in it, counts included; the walk in step 3 catches the failure, and only the volume or the position catches a point that ended up on the other side. For a point on an axis, pass `x=None` or `y=None` to `place`: it aligns the point instead of dimensioning it. For a position that does reach 0, such as the first of a centred row of one, dimension it from a sketch point placed outside the part: a point at x = -100 mm, then the distance `100 mm - (n - 1) / 2 * pitch` from it.
2. **Counts.** Solid patterns take counts 1..1000; a count that reaches 0 fails the rebuild. A fractional count rounds to the nearest whole number without an error (6.5 gives 7 copies), while every other expression uses the exact value, so a centred row shifts. Nothing in SolidCraft enforces a parameter range during a parameter change (configuration rules apply only when a configuration row is activated): choose a range that keeps every count at 1 or more, write "whole number" and the range in the comment, and use `round(n)` wherever the count also positions something.
3. **Circumscribed polygons.** `sketch.polygon.circumscribed` with a size dimension and one vertical side still has 1 dof: its corners can alternate in and out. `sketch.constraint.polygon` makes it regular; `scb.hexagon` adds it.
4. **Boolean retries.** A `Boolean retry: ...` warning means the result may be wrong (see "Boolean warning" in the `solidcraft-modeling` reference), so check the volume of that state. `temporary coincident-face separation` comes from faces that coincide. A tapered tool whose start or end lies on a face of a plain block, or a straight cylinder joined onto the floor of a filleted, shelled box, does not log it; a `tool displacement` warning shows up when a join and a cut share one location, as in a standoff built as a joined cylinder with a cut pilot hole, patterned together. That case reports the warning but its volume agrees with the analytic growth, and a single ring profile removes the warning. Starting cutters about 1 mm past the faces they pierce and sinking joins about 1 mm into the body remain good practice on a single feature. Check the volume of every state either way.
5. **Measurement accuracy.** The `solidcraft-modeling` reference gives how far measured volumes stray from computed ones. Centre of mass and bounding box come out up to about 5e-5 of the part size off. Set test tolerances as the template says.
6. **Expressions.** They have `+ - * / ^ %`, `sin cos tan asin acos atan atan2 sinh cosh tanh asinh acosh atanh sqrt abs min max floor ceil round mod trunc exp ln log log10 pow sign hypot` (`log` is base 10; the hyperbolic ones take and give unit-less numbers), `pi` and units; no `if` and no comparisons. Build steps from `floor`, `mod`, `min`, `max` and `sign`, which gives 1 at 0. `asin acos atan atan2` return angles, so a unitless parameter cannot hold them.
7. **Snapping.** A point created exactly on an existing point or the origin becomes coincident with it (`connect` defaults to true).
8. **Repeated body names.** A repeated `body_name` is renamed (`Body1`) without an error, so `targets` reach only the first body.

## Conventions

- `taper` positive widens along the extrude direction, negative narrows it, also with `direction: negative`.
- `sketch.polygon.circumscribed` with 6 sides and `angle: 0` puts vertices up and down and flat sides facing ±x.
- A pattern of a join or cut feature repeats that join or cut. Put every join before the cuts that must stay open: a later join fills them.
- When a timeline feature fails, `solidcraft-cli run` writes nothing and the error names the feature. `run --in` and `snapshot` also accept a command script in place of a design.
- To build in the user's open app, see the bridged mode in [docs/mcp.md](https://github.com/bherbruck/solidcraft/blob/main/docs/mcp.md): the app and the server both start with extra flags, so ask the user.

name: solidcraft-commands
description: "Use when adding or changing a SolidCraft command or any user-visible behaviour, or when deciding which crate code belongs in. Covers CommandSpec, command ids, programmatic calls vs dialogs, crate layering and the generated feature list."
---

# Adding a command

User-visible behaviour is a command. The toolbar, dialogs, sketch tools, palette, scripts, CLI, control channel and MCP all reach the same commands through `Session::execute(id, params)`. The long form is `docs/book/src/dev/commands.md`.

## Steps
1. Add a `CommandSpec` to the right file in `crates/engine/src/cmd/` and implement `run` (`fn(&mut Session, &Value) -> Result<Value>`). Fields: id, label, toolbar tab and panel (`.at`), icon (`.icon`), shortcut (`.key`), params doc (`.params`), `enabled` (its error string is the disabled-button tooltip).
2. The id is our own: dotted, lower-case `<area>.<thing>[.<variant>]`, such as `solid.extrude` or `sketch.rectangle.two_point`. Never another product's id.
3. Validate inputs first (units, ranges, references) and return `BadParams` rather than building a broken feature. Parameters are hostile: see `skills/solidcraft-crash-safety/SKILL.md`.
4. Give it input and output schemas: a contract and a reply type in `crates/engine/src/schema/`, registered with `checked!`, `.contract` and `.output`. A command should have them and a test warns without them; this will become required. `schema/unconverted.txt` only shrinks. How: `docs/book/src/dev/schemas.md`.
5. Engine tests measure the result: volume, area, face/edge/vertex counts against values you can derive by hand. Where they go: `skills/solidcraft-tests/SKILL.md`.
6. Add the label as `cmd.<command id>` in a pending locale file (`cargo xtask i18n --add-missing` lists what is missing); a test fails without it. See `skills/solidcraft-ui-text/SKILL.md`.
7. A command the ribbon shows also needs help: `help.<command id>` (what it does, then when to use it) in the pending file, and its id in `DOCUMENTED` in `crates/ui-egui/src/command_help.rs`. A test fails without them.
8. Run `cargo xtask features` to see the generated `docs/features.md` change, but do not commit it: `main` regenerates it after each merge.
9. If the command saves something new in a design, add a format file: `skills/solidcraft-file-formats/SKILL.md`.
10. If it needs a dialog or panel: `skills/solidcraft-ui/SKILL.md`.

## Programmatic calls never open dialogs
`engine.execute` runs the JSON form. Only toolbar clicks (`ui.start`) start interactive tools and dialogs, which then run commands. A dialog is a front-end form that builds the parameters.

A command that changes the design is undoable by default (the session snapshots the document first), and a failing command leaves the document unchanged.

## Layering
`cargo xtask layers` fails the build when a lower layer depends on a higher one:

L0 `geom` -> L1 `sketch`, `kernel`, `render` -> L2 `doc` -> L3 `io` -> L4 `engine` -> L5 `ui-egui` -> apps.

- Nothing below L5 depends on egui, eframe, winit, wgpu or rfd. The UI crate is swappable.
- Only `crates/kernel` may use `truck`.
- The UI is thin: panels read engine state and act through `app.run(id, params)` or `app.start(id)`.
- A new module's `mod` line goes into the existing sorted group, not a new group at the end (`cargo fmt` keeps each group sorted).

## Roadmap
`ROADMAP.md` tracks milestones; update it when a milestone task lands.

---
name: solidcraft-contributing
description: Use when someone wants to contribute code or documentation to SolidCraft, from setting up a fork and choosing an issue through submitting a pull request and responding to review.
---

# Contribute to SolidCraft

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) (the router
to the other skills), the [contributor book page](../../docs/book/src/dev/contributing.md),
and the [skills index](../README.md) first. Follow their current rules; use this skill to
help a first-time contributor apply them. This skill concerns the repository,
not modelling a part through MCP.

## Rules for every PR

- **Look at what is open first.** Pull the whole list, drafts included:
  `gh pr list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --limit 500` and
  `gh issue list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --limit 500`. Look for the same issue, the same
  feature under another number, and PRs that change the files you will change
  (`gh pr list ... --json number,title,files`). If someone has it, comment on their PR or issue
  instead of opening a second one: two PRs for one change cannot both land.
- **Claim with a draft PR.** `gh pr list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --search "#N"`; if none,
  branch from the latest `origin/main`, `git commit --allow-empty -m "claim: #N"`, push, and open a
  draft PR titled `<summary> (#N)`. The lowest-numbered open PR for an issue wins; close yours if it
  lost. The bot assigns you and labels the issue `in progress`. Do not claim by editing files; comment
  `/claim` only to stake a claim before you have a branch.
- **Write the title and first sentence for a reader who has seen nothing else.** Not your chat, not the
  issue, not the code. Maintainers pick what to review from the title, and it becomes the commit on
  `main`. Say which part of the app changes and what a user now sees or can do, in everyday words. Don't
  paste the issue's title unless it passes this too. Before opening the PR, and again before marking it
  ready, read both with everything else closed: if "there", "it", "this" or "that" has nothing to point
  at, or a term only makes sense after reading the diff, rewrite it. Keep the terms a user sees in the
  app and explain the others.
  - Unclear: `Send to Slicer: pick one print face per body there, and show print faces only while it is open`
  - Clear: `3D printing: choose the face each body rests on in the Send to Slicer window, not the face menu`
- **Write PR text in plain, literal English.** This follows the spirit of Simplified Technical English,
  not its approved-word list. Keep the names a user sees in the app, even if they aren't everyday words.
  - One idea per sentence, and about 20 words at most.
  - Use active voice: "The view tints the face", not "The face is tinted".
  - Use one word for one thing, and don't switch to a synonym partway through.
  - Repeat the noun when "it" or "this" could be unclear.
  - Don't stack nouns: "the option for picking in the face menu", not "face menu picking option".
- **Push daily.** A draft with no pushes for 72 hours may be taken over: comment first, then open your
  own claim (you may start from its branch). The bot's automatic cleanup deadlines in CONTRIBUTING.md
  are separate.
- **One topic and one issue per PR.** Never commit `plan/`, build directories (`target*/`) or generated
  reference data; check `git ls-files` before pushing. Run `cargo xtask ci` before every commit.
  Commit after every feature arc that builds.
- **Merge flow.** The heavy CI jobs start when a maintainer adds `approved-for-ci`; approved PRs go
  through the merge queue (`gh pr merge N -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --squash --auto`), which runs the
  full suite on each group before it lands on `main`. Never force-push `main`.
- **Do not push only to catch up with `main`** (no merge of `main`, no Update branch, no rebase for
  that alone): every push restarts the whole CI run, and `main`'s own run catches what lands in between.
  When you push anyway, or GitHub reports a conflict, rebase onto the latest `main` and push your own
  branch with `--force-with-lease`; never merge `main` into a PR. Resolve conflicts without discarding
  others' work. Do not re-run CI on an unchanged commit: re-run only a job that runner trouble
  cancelled, with "Re-run failed jobs".
- **Evidence.** For observable CAD, UI or model behaviour (kernel, geometry, assembly and backend
  changes included), the issue or PR carries real screenshots or a short recording from a small
  reproduction, preferably before and after, with steps and expected/actual behaviour. Capture it
  yourself; do not ask a human for evidence you can produce. Diagrams do not replace it. Changes with
  nothing observable need none. Use a public-safe example, check for private designs, paths and account
  details, attach the media rather than committing it.
- **Follow through.** Check the PR's merge status throughout and before handoff. Report the state you
  checked and any conflicts resolved. While the PR is open, keep monitoring it and say clearly that it
  is pending; do not claim it merged without checking.
- **Shared build machine.** Check the load before a big build (`cut -d' ' -f1 /proc/loadavg`), wait
  while it is over 24, and build with `nice`.
- **Maintainers' machines** keep a local, gitignored `plan/` folder: read `plan/STATUS.md` (current
  milestone, next task), then the task in `plan/execution-plan.md` and the relevant `plan/architecture.md`
  section. Kernel and library decisions are in `plan/adr/0001-geometry-kernel.md`. Follow the autonomous
  operation protocol in `plan/execution-plan.md` section 6; do not stop to ask unless it lists the decision
  as the owner's. Contributors without `plan/` can ignore this.
- **Update the roadmap** when a milestone task lands: `docs/roadmap-detail.md` tracks status, milestones and estimates; `ROADMAP.md` is the short user-facing roadmap.
- **Start here.** What to work on: `ROADMAP.md`, "Where help is wanted most" in CONTRIBUTING.md and the open issues labelled `help wanted`, `good first issue`, `needs-triage`; check what is already open first. Architecture: `docs/architecture.md` and "How the code is laid out" in CONTRIBUTING.md; kernel work is paused ("Kernel work is paused" in CONTRIBUTING.md). Licence rules: `deny.toml` and `cargo xtask licences --check`; only `crates/kernel` may use `truck`. When the code, docs and rules settle a question, act; ask on the issue or PR only when the answer changes what users see or what the change covers.
- **Do not open a second PR** for an issue a lower-numbered open PR already closes, and keep the `Changes a default:` line filled in: `pr-checks.yml` fails both.
- **The gate reads the working tree.** Do not switch branches while `cargo xtask ci` runs: it compiles the other branch's code and fails on a change not in the PR. Run it in the background and wait for its log.

## Working as an agent

- **The code is English. The comments are English. Always.** Identifiers, doc comments,
  inline comments, commit messages, branch names, test names, error messages and
  documentation are all in English. This is not a preference: a comment in another
  language is a defect, it is not reviewable by the people who maintain this code, and a
  reviewer rejects it. If something is not obvious, write it in English and keep it
  short. A user-visible string is not inline in the code: it goes to the message
  catalogs in `assets/locales/` (a new one to `assets/locales/pending/<slug>.json`),
  and `skills/solidcraft-ui-text/SKILL.md` says how to name and translate it.
- **Parallel work runs in parallel.** When a task splits into independent parts (several
  files, several areas, several checks that do not depend on each other), dispatch one
  subagent per part and let them run concurrently instead of walking the list one item at
  a time. Give every subagent a self-contained brief: what to change, what not to touch,
  and what to report back. Read the answers before you continue; a subagent's report is
  not a result you can assume.
- **Do not parallelize what depends on itself.** A fix and the test that proves it, a
  refactor and the callers it breaks, two edits to the same file: those stay sequential.
  One subagent per independent unit of work, and no two units may write the same file.

## 1. Check the environment

Explain what you are checking and why, in everyday language. Run:

```sh
gh --version
gh auth status
git --version
rustup show
rustc --version
cargo --version
df -h .
```

Check available memory, CPU and whether a display is available. Establish whether
this is the person's computer or a cloud sandbox; do not assume desktop access,
persistent files or enough space for a full build. Compare Rust with the current
minimum in CONTRIBUTING.md. If tools or sign-in are missing, explain the next
step and help the person set them up; never ask them to paste credentials.

Before every public action, show the exact proposed content and destination and
ask the person to approve it. This includes creating a public fork, pushing,
opening or updating a PR, uploading evidence, marking it ready and commenting.
Explain a PR as a request for maintainers to review a change. Keep check-ins short
at each step: what you found, what comes next, and what needs their decision.

## 2. Fork and clone

Explain that changes go to their own copy on GitHub. After approval, run:

```sh
gh repo fork tangency-labs/solidcraft --clone --remote
cd solidcraft
git remote -v
```

Ensure `origin` points to the person's fork. If `upstream` is absent, add it:

```sh
git remote add upstream https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft.git
```

Never push to upstream. If cloning an existing fork instead, check the same remote
layout. With a clean working tree, sync local `main` before starting work:

```sh
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge --ff-only upstream/main
```

After approval, sync the fork with `git push origin main`. If fast-forwarding
fails, inspect the divergence and preserve existing work; do not reset it away.

## 3. Choose an unclaimed task together

Ask about their interests and show a few issues that fit the available resources.
Read the current kernel-pause notice in CONTRIBUTING.md and skip kernel work
while paused, including tasks outside `crates/kernel/` that change kernel behaviour.
Fetch the whole open list, including drafts, before narrowing it:

```sh
gh issue list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --limit 500
gh pr list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --limit 500 --json number,title,files
gh issue list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --label 'good first issue' --search '-label:kernel-paused -label:"in progress"' --limit 100
gh issue list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --label 'help wanted' --search '-label:kernel-paused -label:"in progress"' --limit 100
```

Let the person choose. Set `N` to that issue's number, then inspect its discussion,
assignee and linked PRs; check similar work under other numbers and overlapping files:

```sh
gh issue view "$N" -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --comments
gh pr list -R tangency-labs/solidcraft --state open --search "#$N"
```

If it is already claimed, choose another task with the person. Do not open a
competing PR or post a comment without their approval.

## 4. Claim with a draft PR

Explain the proposed change and show the draft title and body for approval before
publishing. Recheck availability immediately before claiming. Follow the claim
rules in CONTRIBUTING.md; substitute the chosen summary and fork owner below:

```sh
git fetch upstream
git switch -c "fix-$N" upstream/main
git commit --allow-empty -m "claim: #$N"
git push -u origin "fix-$N"
gh pr create --repo tangency-labs/solidcraft --head "FORK_OWNER:fix-$N" --base main --draft --title "SUMMARY (#$N)" --body-file /tmp/solidcraft-pr-body.md
```

Write the body file first, describing the intended fix and referencing `Fixes #N`.
The draft PR is the claim; check the bot's response and the lowest-numbered open
PR rule before editing. If another claim won, explain it and ask before closing
the duplicate. Do not try to claim by editing files.

## 5. Make and check one focused change

Explain the intended behaviour, then pick the skill for the area from AGENTS.md's table and
follow it (never crash, commands, layering, clean-room rules and tests all live there).
Put synthetic regression tests in the existing test module for the affected area;
prove a bug test fails before the fix and passes after it.

Use the affected crate and test module in commands such as:

```sh
cargo test --profile ci -p solidcraft-engine --lib -- tests::feature_inputs_are_parameters
cargo clippy -p solidcraft-engine --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo xtask ci
```

Run `cargo xtask ci` before each implementation commit on a capable environment.
On small environments, use targeted tests and report exactly what passed and what
could not run; leave the full suite to CI rather than claiming it passed. Follow
[testing guidance](../../docs/book/src/dev/testing.md) for applicable checks.
Review the diff, keep one topic, and commit the finished change. Before an approved
push, follow "Rules for every PR" above; do not push solely to catch up
with `main`. Explain progress and ask before publishing each update.

## 6. Show the result

For visible changes, reproduce the result with a small public-safe example and
capture actual screenshots or a short recording, preferably before and after.
For model output without a display, run:

```sh
solidcraft-cli snapshot script.json --out /tmp/solidcraft-result.png
```

For UI behaviour, launch the desktop app with a free control port:

```sh
cargo run --release -p solidcraft -- --sample --control 7878
```

Follow [the control protocol](../../docs/control-protocol.md): connect to
`127.0.0.1:7878`, read the launch token from its documented location, and send JSON
lines. Put the real token in the first request's top-level `token` field:

```json
{"id":1,"token":"TOKEN","method":"ui.inspect","params":{}}
{"id":2,"method":"ui.screenshot","params":{"path":"/tmp/solidcraft-result.png"}}
```

Use `engine.execute` for commands and `ui.start` plus `ui.click` for interactive
reproductions. Open and inspect the image. Check for private designs, paths and
credentials before sharing; never expose the token. Show the person the media
and ask before attaching it to the PR or linking an accessible recording. Include
brief reproduction steps and expected/actual behaviour; do not commit generated
review media. Documentation-only changes need no screenshot.

## 7. Finish and respond to review

Prepare the final title and body: `Fixes #N`, the problem, resulting behaviour,
validation and any evidence or limitations. Show them to the person before
updating the PR. After their approval, mark the draft ready:

```sh
gh pr ready PR_NUMBER -R tangency-labs/solidcraft
```

Explain that a maintainer reviews the change and adds `approved-for-ci` to start
heavy checks; do not add that label yourself. Monitor checks and merge status,
address review comments, rerun affected checks for fixes, and ask before public
replies or pushes. Report whether it merged or remains pending; do not promise a
merge or rerun an unchanged failing check without evidence of infrastructure trouble.

## Cloud sandbox

Without a display, use `solidcraft-cli snapshot` for model evidence or launch the
app under `Xvfb :99` with `DISPLAY=:99` for UI evidence. With limited disk or CPU,
prefer a documentation or small isolated task, targeted tests and existing build
artifacts; explain any missing checks. Preserve work before temporary storage
expires and ask before publishing it. Always push only to the person's fork,
never to upstream.

name: solidcraft-crash-safety
description: Use when writing or reviewing non-test Rust in SolidCraft, handling design files, command parameters or control-channel input, calling the kernel, or investigating a crash report. A crash loses someone's work, so this outranks feature work.
content:
---
name: solidcraft-crash-safety
description: "Use when writing or reviewing non-test Rust in SolidCraft, handling design files, command parameters or control-channel input, calling the kernel, or investigating a crash report. A crash loses someone's work, so this outranks feature work."
---

# Never crash

People trust SolidCraft with their designs. This outranks feature work.

## In non-test code
- No `unwrap()`, `expect()`, `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `todo!` or `unimplemented!`. Every production crate root carries `#![deny(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used, clippy::panic, clippy::unimplemented, clippy::todo, clippy::unreachable)]`; `cargo xtask ci` runs clippy with `-D warnings`.
- No `unsafe` (`unsafe_code = "forbid"`). The exceptions, in the app crate and in `crates/threedx-client` (which deny it instead), have no safe API:
  - macOS only: `crates/threedx-client/src/macos.rs` (loads the 3Dconnexion driver's client framework at run time and calls through its function pointers), two functions in `apps/solidcraft/src/open_documents.rs` (macOS hands Finder files only to an Objective-C method), and `apps/solidcraft/src/native_crash_macos.rs` (the signal handler that records crashes inside native code, as `native_crash.rs` does on Windows)
  - Windows only: `apps/solidcraft/src/native_crash.rs` (the exception filter that records crashes inside native code such as graphics drivers), `apps/solidcraft/src/native_frame.rs` (the window procedure that answers the resize-border hit test of the window without OS decorations, and gives its class the icon the taskbar falls back on) and `apps/solidcraft/src/space_mouse/windows_hid.rs` (asks Plug and Play which HID interfaces are 3D mice, so no other device is sent anything)
- Errors are `Result<T, E>` through the crate's error type and `?`. An unfinished feature returns an error ("not supported yet: ..."); it never panics.
- Input-derived numbers are hostile (command parameters, design files, control-channel input): `get()` not `[i]`, finite checks, caps on sizes and loop counts.
- Everything that calls `truck` goes through `solidcraft_kernel::guard`, which turns a panic into `KernelError::Internal`. Only `crates/kernel` may use `truck`.
- Last resort: `Session::execute` runs every command under `catch_unwind`; an escaped panic restores the design and reports `EngineError::Internal`. Do not rely on it.
- Files are written with `crates/io/src/safe_write.rs` (temporary file, flush, one rename), so a crash leaves the old file or the new one.

## Proving a crash fix
- Every crash fix lands with a regression test. `hostile_params_never_panic` in `crates/engine/src/tests.rs` runs every command with junk parameters; a new command gets this for free.
- A crash report's `design.sc` and `replay.json` are the test's starting point. Put the test in the area's existing test file (see `skills/solidcraft-tests/SKILL.md`).

## When someone says the app crashed
The desktop app writes every panic and every unclean exit to a local crash folder, with the design and the commands that reproduce it (`solidcraft_engine::crash`, `docs/crash-reports.md`). Look there first:
- `solidcraft-cli crashes`, `solidcraft-cli crashes show <id>`, `solidcraft-cli crashes replay <id>`
- the `diagnostics.crash_reports` command, or the MCP `crash_reports` tool

Crashes and data loss are taken as issues even while kernel work is paused (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Kernel work is paused").

name: solidcraft-editing
description: Use when changing, fixing or extending an existing SolidCraft design through its MCP server - a .sc file (or an older .solidcraft one) or the design open in the app. Typical requests: resize it, move a cut, change a hole or standoff, add a fillet or chamfer, make a fixed value parametric, or a feature shows an error after a change or after the app crashed.
content:
---
name: solidcraft-editing
description: "Use when changing, fixing or extending an existing SolidCraft design through its MCP server - a .sc file (or an older .solidcraft one) or the design open in the app. Typical requests: resize it, move a cut, change a hole or standoff, add a fillet or chamfer, make a fixed value parametric, or a feature shows an error after a change or after the app crashed."
---

# SolidCraft editing

## Overview
Edit an existing design through its parameters instead of rebuilding it. Every sketch dimension and feature input is already a parameter (`d1`, `d2`, ...), so most edits are a `parameters.change` each, sent together in one batch. Map the design with a few compact calls rather than walking the timeline one feature at a time. For command shapes and traps, in SolidCraft's own chat or any MCP client, call `skill_reference {"skill":"solidcraft-modeling"}`. Elsewhere, use `reference.md` from the `solidcraft-modeling` skill.

## Map the design (3-4 calls)
1. **Open:** if the design is not open yet, run `open {path}`. When the server is bridged to the app and the current design is `dirty`, ask before opening anything.
2. **Overview:** `inspect_design {"measure":false,"sketches":false}` lists the user parameters, the sketch dimensions (`d1`, `d2`, ... with their expressions), the features in order, and their errors.
3. **Feature inputs:** `execute parameters.list {"filter":"feature"}` gives every feature input as an object such as `{"name":"d9","expression":"(6) / 2","feature":"Cylinder1","input":"Radius"}`. `inspect_design` leaves these out.
   - Match sketch dimensions by expression.
   - If that is ambiguous, `sketch.inspect {sketch}` that one sketch, which also shows its points in world coordinates.
4. **Baseline:** `measure {}`, so you can predict every change against it.

`timeline.inspect {feature}` is only for two cases:
- changing more than a number: profiles, direction, operation or edges
- checking whether a position follows a parameter, for example a cylinder `base` written as `width/2 - wall - 6`

Inspect one feature of each kind, not every copy.

## Change
- **A number:** `parameters.change {"name":"d9","expression":"..."}`.
  - **To make a fixed value parametric:** add a user parameter first (`parameters.add standoff_d`), then set each input to an expression of it (`standoff_d/2`).
  - **Several changes:** one `batch`.
- **A user parameter:** `set_parameter` or `parameters.change`. Every expression that uses it follows.
- **Structure:** `timeline.edit {"feature":..., "set":{...}}`, with the field shapes `timeline.inspect` shows.
- **A new feature** goes at the end of the timeline. To place it earlier:
  1. `timeline.roll_to {"position":N}`. A position is safer than a name, since a sketch and a feature can share one.
  2. Add the feature.
  3. `timeline.roll_to {}` to return to the end.

  Everything after the insert recomputes, and a feature that worked can now fail. Seen: a corner fillet after an inserted chamfer.
- **Risky or multi-step edits:** take `edit.checkpoint` in its own call first. `edit.restore_checkpoint {checkpoint}` goes back exactly. Restoring uses the checkpoint up (and any later ones): take a new one to go back again. Only the last 16 are kept. A `batch` rolls itself back; separate `execute` calls do not.
- **Deleting:** `timeline.dependents {feature}` first. It lists what is deleted with it and what would fail.
- **Ambiguous wording:** "2 mm higher" on a value written as `wall + 6` can be relative (`wall + 8`) or absolute.
  - Keep the design's intent, which is the relative reading.
  - Tell the user which reading you used. This matters most when the same request also changes `wall`, because then the two readings give different heights.
- **New constants** such as a chamfer size go in user parameters, so the user can change them later.

## Verify
1. **Predict, then measure once.** Send the independent changes in one batch, predict the total volume change, then run `measure` once.
   - A move does not change the volume. To confirm a moved sketch, read its points' world coordinates with `sketch.inspect`. You can also predict the COM shift, `Δcom = V_moved · Δz / V_body`, but only when nothing else in that batch changes the volume.
   - If it matches to about 0.01%, you are done.
   - If not, restore the checkpoint, take a new one, then apply the changes one at a time, measuring after each.
   - A cut or chamfer that leaves the volume unchanged has missed.
2. **Timeline health:** run `inspect_design {"measure":false,"sketches":false}`. Every `error` and `warning` must be null. If something broke, restore or `undo` before you try anything else.
3. **Interior features:** take one top-view screenshot, `{"source":"model","view":"top","width":480,"height":320}`. When the server is bridged, `view` also turns the user's camera. The iso view hides standoffs behind the walls.
4. **Still parametric:** if the user wants it kept parametric, change one driving size, `measure`, then set it back.

## When something is already broken
- **A feature has an `error` after opening:** read it with `timeline.inspect`, fix the input or definition, and recompute.
- **The app crashed:**
  - `crash_reports` lists the reports, and `crash_reports {id}` gives the command that crashed.
  - `execute doc.recovery_list` and then `doc.recover {id}` reopen the autosaved design.
  - Never retry the crashing command unchanged.

## Save
`save {"path":"...-v2.sc"}` writes a copy. `save {}` overwrites the opened file; do that only when the user asked for it.

## Red flags

| Thought | Do instead |
|---|---|
| "timeline.inspect each feature to understand it" | `parameters.list {"filter":"feature"}` shows every input in one call. |
| "Delete and remodel the feature" | Change its `dN` input, or use `timeline.edit`. History and downstream picks stay intact. |
| "The insert worked, done" | Check the errors of every later feature. |
| "Edge points with expressions, so the chamfer follows the size" | They are rejected, and stored picks already follow size changes. |
| "Pick all 8 rim edges" | One pick on a tangent chain fillets or chamfers the whole chain. |
| "Measure after every edit" | One batch, one `measure` against the summed prediction. Split only when it misses. |

name: solidcraft-file-formats
description: Use when a SolidCraft change saves something new in a design (a field, a feature type, a kind of name) or changes what older designs mean, and when touching STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ, DXF or URDF import and export.
content:
---
name: solidcraft-file-formats
description: "Use when a SolidCraft change saves something new in a design (a field, a feature type, a kind of name) or changes what older designs mean, and when touching STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ, DXF or URDF import and export."
---

# Design file format, import and export

## Design file format changes
A design says which format it is in (`"format": "solidcraft/N"`). A change that saves something new, or makes older designs mean something else, adds ONE file and edits nothing shared:

1. Create `crates/doc/src/format/pending/<what-it-is>.rs` (lowercase, dashes). Start it with a `//!` note: what is saved, what older designs get without it, and that the last release opens such a design with a warning and keeps what it can't read (`crates/doc/src/newer_file.rs`).
2. If older designs must be rewritten as they open, put `pub fn step(v: &mut Value) -> crate::Result<()>` in the same file. Pending steps run in file-name order, after the older formats' steps.
3. Never touch `FORMAT`, `JSON_STEPS`, the history in `crates/doc/src/format.rs`, another change's file, or any `v<N>/` folder. The build counts the pending files and writes the next number, so a release knows a design carries a change it doesn't have: it warns, and saving keeps the file's number and what it couldn't read.

Two PRs that each add a change merge without a conflict. `crates/doc/src/format/pending/README.md` has an example. At release time the maintainer runs `scripts/fold-format-pending.sh`, which moves pending files into `v<N>/` for good; `scripts/test-format-pending.sh` runs in CI. Never add a file to a `v<N>/` folder afterwards. See `docs/releasing.md`.

Drawings follow the same rules with their own numbers, from 1: a drawing-format change is ONE new file in `crates/doc/src/drawing/format/pending/` (see its `README.md`), and the same fold script moves them into `crates/doc/src/drawing/format/v<N>/`.

## Import
- Every import (STEP, IGES, 3MF, STL, OBJ; inserted, dropped, opened, or run as `file.insert_step`, `file.insert_mesh` or `doc.open`) becomes a new component named after the file, with the Import feature inside it. Bodies never land loose.
- Imported files are untrusted: sizes, entity counts and nesting are capped, and every kernel call is guarded (`skills/solidcraft-crash-safety/SKILL.md`). What cannot be read becomes a warning on the feature.
- STEP is read by our own reader in `crates/kernel/src/step_in`, written from the public standards, with no third-party STEP code. The reader and what it supports: `docs/step-import.md`.
- Imported assemblies are rigid by default; Unlock Contents releases them.
- Kernel work (booleans, STEP/IGES import and export, tessellation) is paused except crashes and data loss: CONTRIBUTING.md, "Kernel work is paused".

## Export
- STEP, 3MF, STL, OBJ and URDF go through `file.export` and `file.save_mesh`; the MCP `export` tool calls them. URDF: `docs/urdf.md`. 3MF face tags: `docs/formats/3mf-face-tags.md`.
- Mesh and design readers and writers live in `crates/io/src/`. Write files through `crates/io/src/safe_write.rs`.
- Reference tests for exports never take their expected values from SolidCraft's own output (`skills/solidcraft-tests/SKILL.md`).

name: solidcraft-ground-rules
description: Use before adding any dependency, icon, image, font, test reference data or product wording to SolidCraft, or when unsure whether something may be copied, read or named. Covers independence from other CAD products, GPL code, asset attribution and the product name.
content:
---
name: solidcraft-ground-rules
description: "Use before adding any dependency, icon, image, font, test reference data or product wording to SolidCraft, or when unsure whether something may be copied, read or named. Covers independence from other CAD products, GPL code, asset attribution and the product name."
---

# Independence, licences, assets and the name

The rules that cannot be broken in a PR. `AGENTS.md` lists them in one line each; the reasons are in CONTRIBUTING.md, "Rules that aren't negotiable".

## Independent
- Behaviour comes from public documentation, general CAD conventions and user feedback. File formats come from public specifications.
- Never copy another product's code, icons, artwork, help text, tooltips, templates or materials.
- Reference tests use analytic values (`tools/oracle-analytic/`) or open-source tools. Expected values never come from a commercial CAD product.
- Do not drive, script, automate or extract data from commercial CAD products (Fusion, SolidWorks, Onshape, ...) for this project: no test data, measurements, command lists, ids or files produced with them.
- Command ids are our own: dotted, lower-case `<area>.<thing>[.<variant>]`, never another product's id.

## No GPL, LGPL or AGPL code
- Do not read, copy or link OpenCASCADE, FreeCAD (including planegcs), SolveSpace, CadQuery/OCP, LibreCAD or QCAD. Do not even read their sources.
- `tools/freecad-oracle/` runs FreeCAD as a separate program through its public scripting API to compute reference values. Nothing from FreeCAD is linked, vendored or shipped. The sketch solver and the blend operations are our own.
- Permissive dependencies are fine: say which one you add and why in the PR. `THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.txt` is regenerated on `main`; never edit it in a PR (`cargo xtask licences --check` only reports).
- Code adapted from other permissive projects (MIT OR Apache-2.0) is noted in ATTRIBUTION.md. Projects published by [storytold](https://github.com/storytold) can serve as references for implementation conventions.

## Assets: the most serious rule
- SolidCraft contains no iconography, images, fonts or artwork from commercial CAD products, ever. Screenshots of commercial CAD software are never committed.
- Every file asset is original or openly licensed and has a row in ATTRIBUTION.md. `cargo xtask assets` enforces it.
- Command icons are the original SVG masters in `assets/icons/ui/design/svg/`, compiled through `crates/ui-egui/src/icon_svg.rs`.
- Before any icon, icon assignment or media edit, read `assets/AGENTS.md`, `assets/icons/ui/AGENTS.md` and `assets/icons/ui/STYLE_GUIDE.md`. Use the canonical bases and named finished references there; never invent a parallel icon style. `cargo xtask icons` validates them.

## The name
- SolidCraft everywhere: crates `solidcraft-*`, binaries `solidcraft` and `solidcraft-cli`, `.sc` designs (`.solidcraft` still opens), the `solidcraft/N` format tag, `SOLIDCRAFT_*` environment variables, settings and recovery folders, the MCP server name, docs, CI and packaging.
- The old name survives only in the compatibility shims listed in `docs/compatibility.md`. Do not add new uses of it.
- Public docs, web and Flatpak deployments use project Pages `/solidcraft/`. Do not add permanent old-name Pages aliases.
- Labels, parameter docs, messages and docs use the terms in the glossary (`docs/book/src/reference/glossary.md`): one term for each idea. A change that adds a new idea adds its term there.
- Units are millimetres and radians internally; Z is up.

content:
---
name: solidcraft-mechanisms
description: Use when building, driving or animating an assembly or mechanism in SolidCraft through its MCP server - components, grounding, joints and joint origins, rigid groups, motion links, closed loops such as an actuator on a hinged panel or a linkage, contact sets, motion studies, degrees of freedom - or when a drive moves nothing, stops early or a part jumps when it is joined. To model the parts themselves, use solidcraft-modeling.
---

# SolidCraft mechanisms

## Overview
An assembly is components placed by joints. Work the mechanism out as world points and axes first: every pin, slide and hinge, which part each one joins, and the value you expect at each pose. Then give every joint origin by those coordinates, and check each step against a number you computed yourself. A drive that reports success can still have moved nothing. Command shapes, a worked example, the traps and reply sizes are in `reference.md` next to this file. To build the parts themselves, use `solidcraft-modeling`.

Written against SolidCraft `main` after 0.11.1, which counts the degrees of freedom of closed loops, carries motion links through chains made in any order, and answers drives in degrees with `moved` (and a `reason` when nothing could move).

## Before the first call
1. In SolidCraft's own chat or any MCP client, call `skill_reference {"skill":"solidcraft-mechanisms"}`. Elsewhere, read `reference.md`.
2. **Open:** if the design is not open yet, run `open {path}`. When the server is bridged to the app and the current design is `dirty`, ask before opening anything.
3. **Map it:** run `inspect_design {"measure":false,"sketches":false}`, then `execute joint.list`. `joint.list` shows `fixed` (the grounded occurrences, always with the root, 0), `dof` per occurrence, `conflicts`, the joints, links and named origins, at about 0.5 KB per joint. `execute motion.list` lists the motion studies.
4. **Existing design:** take `edit.checkpoint` in its own call before you move bodies into components. `edit.restore_checkpoint {checkpoint}` goes back exactly, once: restoring uses the checkpoint up, so take a new one to go back again.
5. **Write the plan:**
   - the components, and which one is grounded
   - each joint: type, the two occurrences, its world point and axis, limits
   - each motion link and its ratio
   - for each loop, the relation you will check, such as actuator stroke against hinge angle, and where it should stop
   - the pose to return to before saving

## Build, in stages
1. **Components and grounding.**
   - Bodies made in the root go into components with `component.create {"name":..., "parent":"root", "activate":false}`, then `component.move_bodies {"bodies":[...], "component":...}`.
   - A part that moves in two pieces, such as an actuator's barrel and rod, becomes two components.
   - Ground the base: `occurrence.ground {"occurrence":"Frame:1", "grounded":true}`. The design's first top-level part is grounded when it is made; check `joint.list` `fixed`, and unground it (`"grounded":false`) if it is not the base. A grounded part refuses `occurrence.move`. Occurrences are named `<component>:<n>`. Joint commands also take a component name (its first occurrence); `occurrence.ground` does not.
2. **Open-chain joints in one batch.** Read `occurrence.properties` of each moving occurrence before the batch and after it. If something moved, split the batch to find the joint.
3. **Each joint that closes a loop, in a call of its own.** Then check `conflicts` in its reply.
4. **Motion links.**
5. **Contact sets and the motion study.**

## Joints
- **Origins by world coordinates:** `{"occurrence":..., "point":[x,y,z], "z":[ax,ay,az]}`. Always give `occurrence`; without it the nearest body is used. Use the same form on both sides; `frame`, `face`, `circle` and named origins are in `reference.md`.
- **Pass `flip: true`** when both origins are the same world point and axis, which is the case when you join parts where they sit. Without it, b's z mates against a's and part b turns 180 degrees.
- **Parts already in place:** `joint.as_built {"type":..., "a":..., "b":..., "at":{origin}, "name":..., "limits":[[min,max]]}` keeps them where they are.
- **Values and limits** are degrees for angles and mm for distances. An angle turns right-handed about the joint's z. A drive past a joint's own limits is clamped to them, which is not a failure. A new joint starts at its `values` (default 0); one outside the limits starts at the nearer limit, so the part turns there as it is joined, and the reply's `warnings` say so. `value` drives a joint's first value and `values` the ones it lists; the others keep theirs.
- **Every chain must reach something grounded.** A part that is neither grounded nor joined to a grounded part is never placed. A drive on a joint in that chain moves nothing and answers `moved: false`, with a `reason` and the part joined to nothing as `unconnected`. `joint.list` lists such chains under `floating`, and their occurrences have `dof: 6`. Fix it with `joint.rigid_group {"occurrences":["Frame:1", ...]}`, or with a joint to the grounded structure.

## Linked and closed motion
- **Motion links:** `joint.motion_link {"a":..., "b":..., "ratio":r, "offset":o}` sets b = r·a + o, clamped to b's own limits. `ratio` is b's units per a's: a pinion that moves its rack 0.5 mm per degree takes `ratio: 0.5`. `offset` is in b's units: degrees for an angle, mm for a distance, or an expression. A mirrored part takes `ratio: -1`, and limits mirrored too. Chains (a drives b, b drives c) work in any order of creation. Drive only the head of a chain.
- **Gears, racks and screws:** links whose ratio comes from radii or a pitch, kept up to date when they change. `joint.gear {"a":..., "b":..., "ra":r1, "rb":r2}` turns b r1/r2 as far as a, the other way (`internal: true`: the same way). `joint.rack_pinion {"a":pinion, "b":rack, "radius":r}` moves the rack r·θ. `joint.screw {"joint":cylindrical, "pitch":p}` (or `a`, `b` for a revolute and a slider) advances p per turn. A size is mm, an expression (`"m*z1/2"`), or a round face `{"occurrence":..., "circle":[x,y,z]}` whose radius is read again after every edit. `reverse: true` turns b the other way (a left-hand thread). The driven joint keeps where it is. Drive a, never b.
- **Cams:** `joint.cam {"a":camJoint, "b":follower, "profile":{"sketch":"CamSketch"}}` (or `{"edges":[[x,y,z]]}` on the cam's body) makes a slider or revolute follower ride the cam's outline. `follower`: `knife` (default), `roller` with `radius` (mm, an expression or the roller's round face), `flat`. A revolute follower needs `tip` (its knife's point or roller's centre). The table is worked out again after every edit; the follower keeps where it is, so model it touching. Drive the cam, never the follower.
- **Closed loops:** an actuator between a frame and a hinged panel takes three joints besides the hinge:
  - a revolute root pin (frame and barrel)
  - a slider (barrel and rod), with z along the actuator from root to tip on both origins, both at the root pin, and the stroke as its limits
  - a revolute tip pin (rod and panel), which closes the loop

  A four-bar or a slider-crank follows the same pattern. Drive the hinge; the pins and the slider follow.
- **Stops:** at the end of the stroke the drive stops, with `stopped_by_loop: {joint, fraction}` naming the joint that could not follow. A loop that cannot close at all is listed under `conflicts`, and nothing in it moves.
- **dof** counts the loop: here the panel, barrel and rod report 1 each, also at a pose where the actuator lies along its tip pin's path.

## Contact and motion studies
- **Contact:** `contact.create {"occurrences":[...], "name":...}` and `contact.enable_sets {}`. A drive then stops where two bodies of one set would pass through each other, with `stopped_by_contact: {a, b, fraction}`. `contact.check {}` lists the pairs that overlap now.
- **Motion study:** `motion.study {"name":..., "steps":N, "keys":[{"joint":..., "points":[[step, value], ...]}]}`. Values are degrees or mm, linear between points. Key only the driving joints; linked joints and loops follow.
- **Play:** `motion.play {"study":..., "step":s}` sets the joints there, which changes the design, and answers every occurrence's pose (about 0.2 KB per occurrence). `motion.export {"study":..., "samples":n}` gives the poses at every step without changing the design.
- **Trace:** `motion.trace {"occurrence":..., "point":[x,y,z], "joint":..., "from":0, "to":360}` (or `"study":...` instead of joint, from and to) answers the world path of a point of a part, such as a coupler curve, without changing the design. It ends at `stopped_at` where a loop or contact stops the motion. `motion.trace.keep` with the same params keeps it as a 3D sketch spline.
- **Plot:** `motion.plot {"study":..., "joints":[...], "duration":seconds}` answers each joint value's `value`, `velocity` and `acceleration` per sample (finite differences; per step, or per second with a duration), and with `"occurrence"` and `"point"` a point's `position`, `velocity`, `acceleration`, `speed`. Check a follower's rate against the analytic one this way, without changing the design.
- **Collisions:** `motion.interference {"study":..., "occurrences":[...], "against":[...]}` plays the study (contact sets don't stop it) and lists each colliding pair with `first_step` and `steps` ranges; `clear: true` when none and every step was checked (never while `truncated`: then it stopped at `checked_to`; give a gear train or other detailed parts more time with `budget_s`). It takes at most 256 bodies: on a big design list the moving part as `occurrences` and what it must miss as `against`. Parts joined at a knuckle often overlap by design and show up at every step.
- **Sweep until contact:** `joint.sweep {"joint":..., "from":0, "to":120, "occurrences":[...], "against":[...], "report_gaps":true}` answers how far a hinge, door or linkage opens: `stopped_at` (last clear value, bisected to `refine` mm, default 0.01), `stopped_by` `{a, b, at}` (or `"loop"`, `"limit"`), per-sample `min_gap_mm` and the nearest each part came (`min_gap`). It runs on a copy; `"apply":true` leaves the design at the stop. Pairs touching at `from` (`touching_at_start`) stop it only once they pass into each other.
- **Find limits:** `joint.find_limits {"joint":...}` sweeps each value both ways from where it is (its own limits ignored, on a copy) and answers per value `min`, `max`, `min_by`/`max_by` (`{a, b, at}`, `"loop"`, `"limit"`, `"turn"`: nothing met within a turn, `"range"`: a distance meets nothing, `null` value). Set the joint's limits from it with `joint.limits`. A full turn of curved parts resting in each other can take a few seconds.

## Verify
- **Each joint:** `execute occurrence.properties {"occurrence":"Wing:1"}` (about 2 KB) gives the world bbox, centre of mass and inertia of one occurrence. Joining must not move them.
- **Each drive:** compute the expected value of every follower, and read it back from `joint.list` (degrees and mm, with `unit`). For an actuator from root R to tip T on a panel hinged at H: `L(θ) = |T(θ) - R|`, where `T(θ)` is T turned by θ about the hinge axis through H, and the stroke is `L(θ) - L(0)`. A closed loop matches to 1e-6 mm.
- **Each stop:** solve for where the limit is reached, and compare with the value the drive stopped at. Stops are found by bisection, so they land within about 0.01 degrees.
- **Links:** b must equal r·a + o exactly, unless that is outside b's limits; then b sits at the limit and the mirror stops following.
- **The whole motion:** `motion.play` at a few steps, or one `motion.export`, and compare the poses with the values you planned.
- **Look:** when the server is bridged, `screenshot` after `motion.play` shows the app window at that step. `motion.export_animation {"study":..., "path":"tour.gif"}` (or `joint`, `from`, `to`) writes the whole motion as an animated GIF without changing the design.

## Save
- Drive the joints back to the pose you planned to keep (`motion.play` at step 0, or `joint.drive`), then `save {path}`.
- An `.urdf` export leaves out each joint that closes a loop, because URDF is a tree.

## Red flags

| Thought | Do instead |
|---|---|
| "The origins are at the same point, so `flip` doesn't matter" | Pass `flip: true`, or the part turns 180 degrees. |
| "The drive answered values, so it moved" | Read `moved`; a chain joined to nothing grounded answers `moved: false` and a `reason`. |
| "Drive the arm joint by joint until the gripper gets there" | `joint.reach {"occurrence":..., "at":..., "point":...}` solves every joint on its chain at once; read `reached` and `error_mm`. |
| "Key every joint of the loop in the study" | Key the driving joint only; the loop follows. |
| "Check the pose with `component.list`" | `occurrence.properties` on the one occurrence. `component.list` is 140 KB on a 36-part assembly. |
| "Open the design with `file.open`" | The `open` tool, or `doc.open`; there is no `file.open`. |

name: solidcraft-modeling
description: Use when building a new part, enclosure, bracket, plate, flange or any other 3D solid in SolidCraft through its MCP server (tools such as batch, execute, measure, screenshot), or when a SolidCraft session is using many tool calls or tokens.
content:
---
name: solidcraft-modeling
description: Use when building a new part, enclosure, bracket, plate, flange or any other 3D solid in SolidCraft through its MCP server (tools such as batch, execute, measure, screenshot), or when a SolidCraft session is using many tool calls or tokens.
---

# SolidCraft modeling

## Overview
Work the part out as numbers first. Then build it in a few large `batch` calls, and check each stage with `measure` against values you computed yourself. A clean build takes 3-4 build batches, about 10-13 calls with the checks. Command shapes, plane axes, ids, reply sizes and known traps are in `reference.md` next to this file, so you do not need to explore the command catalog.

## Before the first call
1. In SolidCraft's own chat or any MCP client, call `skill_reference {"skill":"solidcraft-modeling"}`. Elsewhere, read `reference.md`.
2. Run `inspect_design {"measure":false,"sketches":false}`, even when you think the session is empty.
   - The SolidCraft server's instructions end with `Backend: connected to the SolidCraft app` when it drives the user's open app, and with `Backend: headless` otherwise.
   - If the design has timeline features, ask before calling `new_design` or `open`, because both discard unsaved work. You can also build into the open design.
3. Write a plan:
   - the parameters
   - the placement: centre the part on the origin so patterns and mirrors can work from the planes
   - every feature, with the world point you will use for each edge or face pick
   - the expected volume and bounding box

## Build
- **Stages:** use one batch per stage:
  1. parameters, sketch, dimensions, finish and the first feature
  2. fillets and shell
  3. holes, cuts and patterns
- **Failures:** a batch is all-or-nothing. On failure, read `failed.index` and `failed.error`, fix that step only, and send the batch again.
- **Risky steps:** put a risky step in a batch of its own, so a failure does not roll back the work around it. This covers booleans between curved faces that touch, and anything you have not done before.
- **Reply size:** in large designs, pass `"verbose": false` to `batch` and `execute`.
- **Sketch ids are predictable,** so later steps in the same batch can use them:
  - Each sketch counts each kind from 1 (`l1`, `c1`, `a1`, `p1`).
  - Count what the earlier steps of that sketch created. For example, `rectangle.center` makes `l1`-`l6` and `p1`-`p5`.
  - Do not split a batch just to read ids back.
- **Positions that must follow a parameter** come from:
  - sketch dimensions to `"origin"` with expression values (`"w/2 - wall - 6"`)
  - expression fields such as `solid.cylinder base:["w/2-6","d/2-6","wall"]`

  A plain number never follows a parameter.
- **Repeats:** `solid.pattern.rectangular` takes expression spacing; `solid.mirror` takes `XY`/`XZ`/`YZ`, a construction plane or `{origin, normal}` (origin coordinates may be length expressions such as `["half", 0, 0]`). A mirror or pattern feature cannot be mirrored or patterned again.
- **Edge and face picks** snap to the nearest edge or face. An edge pick farther than 5% of the body's size from every edge is refused (`the nearest edge is 15.000 mm away`). On a large body that limit is wide (about 48 mm on a 949 mm board), so compute the exact midpoint from your geometry (the vertical corner edge of a centred box is `[w/2, d/2, h/2]`).
  - Picks must be plain numbers.
  - A pick is resolved once and then follows its edge when parameters change.
  - A face can be given by name instead of a point (`faces:["F1:+z"]`, the `face` of `sheet.convert`). `body_topology` lists each face's `name`, a `point` that lies on it (the centroid of a face with a hole is in the hole) and, for a cylinder, `{origin, axis, radius}`.
- **Profiles:** extrude takes every region by default, and a region inside another is a hole in it: two concentric circles give a ring. A third circle inside the ring gives a separate disc body. Pass `profiles` to choose regions.
- **Order:** fillet the outside edges before you shell, so the shell follows the fillets. There are two exceptions:
  - An edge of the face the shell removes, such as the rim of an open box: round it after the shell, because the shell can fail on it.
  - A fillet between two curved faces, such as a sphere joined to a cylinder: the shell then fails with `offset: only bodies with planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori`. Shell first. The inside corner then stays sharp, so the wall there is thinner than `thickness`.

## Verify
- **Each stage:** run `measure {}` (about 0.9 KB per body; `{"summary":true}` keeps only name, volume, bbox, face count and `closed` per body) and compare the volume, bbox and face count with your numbers. A cut or hole that leaves the volume unchanged has missed, even though it reported success.
- **Timeline health:** `inspect_design {"measure":false,"sketches":false}` shows each feature's `error` and `warning`.
- **Parameter test:** run `set_parameter`. Expect `errors: []`, then `measure` again; the COM and bbox should move by the amounts you computed. To try values without keeping them, `check_parameters {"set": {"L": "140 mm"}}` reports the volume, errors and cylinder axes and puts the design back.
- **Positions:** `measure` does not say where a feature sits.
  - On an asymmetric part, check the COM shift you computed.
  - On a symmetric part (a mirrored or patterned layout) the COM does not move, so take a top-view screenshot and compare distances in pixels against a known size.
  - For holes and bosses, `body_topology {"body":"Body1","faces":"cylinders"}`: one entry per cylinder (`radius`, `origin`, `axis`, `extent` along the axis, the merged faces' `names`), a few lines.
  - The full `body_topology` is a last resort: it costs 25-45 KB and splits cylinders into half faces.
- **Final look:** one `screenshot {"source":"model","view":"iso","width":480,"height":320}`. Use `"view":"top"` for features inside walls, which the iso view hides.
  - `width` and `height` apply only to model renders.
  - When the server is bridged, `source` defaults to the whole app window and `view` also turns the user's camera, so pass `"source":"model"` and leave out `view` unless the user wants the camera moved.

## Finish
`export {path}` writes `.step` for CAD, `.3mf`/`.stl` for printing, or `.urdf` (an assembly with joints, for robot simulators). `save {path}` writes `.sc` (`.solidcraft` files from earlier releases still open).

## Red flags

| Thought | Do instead |
|---|---|
| "List all commands first" | `reference.md`, or `list_commands {"filter":"<distinctive word>"}`. The unfiltered list is over 100 KB. |
| "Check positions with body_topology" | `measure` COM and bbox against your numbers. |
| "Inspect the sketch" | `sketch.solve` returns dof and the profile count in under 100 bytes. Run `sketch.inspect` on its own, never inside a big batch. |
| "new_design for a clean start" | When the server is bridged, ask first. |
| "It reported ok, so it worked" | Only a `measure` that matches the computed values counts. |

name: solidcraft-packaging
description: "Use when preparing or shipping a SolidCraft release, changing installers or packages (AppImage, MSI, dmg, Flatpak, Snap, WinGet, Nix, FreeBSD, web), release asset names, signing or the Pages deployment."
---

# Packaging and releases

Development pushes are not application releases. Pushing to `main` or pushing a tag does not start a release. The full procedure is `docs/releasing.md`; follow it when asked to prepare or ship a release.

## Preparing
1. Choose one version for the whole batch from the actual changes (patch, minor, major, `-rc.N`). Do not infer it from commit prefixes. Moving to `1.0` is the owner's decision.
2. Update `[workspace.package] version` in `Cargo.toml`, then `cargo update --workspace --offline`; only our own crates' `version =` lines in `Cargo.lock` change.
3. Fold the pending design-format changes with `scripts/fold-format-pending.sh` (`skills/solidcraft-file-formats/SKILL.md`).
4. Run `cargo xtask ci` and the packaging checks in `.github/workflows/packaging-lint.yml`. Land the version commit on `main` through the normal review flow; never use `[skip ci]`.

## Building and publishing
- Advance the `release` branch with fast-forwards only (`git merge --ff-only`); never force-push. `.github/workflows/release.yml` builds every package and creates a draft GitHub Release.
- Verify the draft before publishing: the run succeeded for the intended SHA, every platform and architecture is present, `sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS.txt` passes, and the built CLI runs (`--version`, an example model).
- Only when shipping is authorised, publish the verified draft with `gh release edit`, then confirm its tag resolves to the recorded SHA and the downstream deployment ran. A request to prepare a release is not a request to publish.
- Never overwrite a published version, tag or asset; use a new version. Do not push the version tag yourself. Packages are unsigned unless `docs/releasing.md` says otherwise; do not claim they are signed.
- Nightlies are prereleases built by the same workflow; they never become latest or advance `release`.

## Names that must stay stable
- Assets are `solidcraft-<version>-...` and are also attached without the version (`solidcraft-windows-x64.msi`). The README links and the in-app update check (`crates/ui-egui/src/update.rs`) pick them by name; renaming one breaks both.
- The old product name survives only in the shims in `docs/compatibility.md`. Do not rewrite published assets, checksums, tags or historical notes.
- Documentation, the browser app and the Flatpak repository publish under project Pages `/solidcraft/`. Add no old-name Pages aliases.

## Where things live
- `packaging/` holds the per-platform scripts (`packaging/linux`, `packaging/windows`, `packaging/macos`, `packaging/freebsd`, `packaging/web`); `packaging/tests` checks them.
- Nix: `flake.nix` and `docs/nix.md`. Building: `docs/building.md`. Downloads: `docs/downloads.md`.
- Build with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=<repo>/target`. Windows from Linux: `cargo xwin build --release --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p solidcraft`.

name: solidcraft-performance
description: "Use when a SolidCraft change is slow, blocks the window, runs long work, or must build for the browser. Covers keeping the window thread free, measuring a speed-up, the wasm build and what may be JavaScript or Python."
---

# Performance, threads and wasm

## Do not block the window
- Work that can take long (a feature computation, a save, a file load, reading a picture) runs beside the window and is applied when done. Existing examples: `crates/ui-egui/src/save_job.rs`, `crates/ui-egui/src/file_load.rs`, and the agent path in `docs/control-protocol.md` ("Slow commands and the window").
- With the preference "Keep the window responsive while agents run commands" (`agent_off_thread`) on, a design change that takes longer than about 150 ms is evaluated ahead on a copy of the design, then run for real reusing that result. A person's edit made meanwhile goes first; Stop drops the computation and nothing is applied. Keep that contract when you add a long-running command.
- `file.export` and `file.save_mesh` change nothing in the design: they run on a copy and nothing waits behind them.
- Test it: `crates/ui-egui/src/apply_off_thread_tests.rs` drives a long feature through the harness; never depend on wall-clock timing in a test.

## Measure before you claim a speed-up
- Profile first. Time with `solidcraft-cli` from `main` and from your branch, alternating runs, after the load is low. On a shared machine check `cut -d' ' -f1 /proc/loadavg` and wait while it is over 24; build with `nice`.
- Report medians with the range, the machine, and the cases. The pattern to follow is `docs/perf.md`: what was slow, why, the result, and proof that nothing changed (same bodies, volumes, areas and triangle counts).
- A speed-up never skips work on a mesh's box: decide with the exact bounds (`Body::exact_bounds`, grown by the record's tolerance as `apart` in `crates/kernel/src/ops.rs` does). A mesh is for display, export, previews and mesh bodies.
- Do not rewrite kernel code for speed: the kernel is being replaced, and kernel work is paused. Report a slow case with its file under the `kernel-perf` label (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Where help is wanted most").
- Pull requests run only the tests for what they touch; geometry-heavy tests run in the merge queue. Use `cargo xtask test` with the `ci` profile locally (`skills/solidcraft-tests/SKILL.md`).

## The browser build
- Everything below the apps must build for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`: `cargo xtask wasm` checks every library crate and the web app, and is part of `cargo xtask ci`. Do not add a dependency that cannot.
- Application code is Rust only. The browser requires two pieces of JavaScript: the service worker `apps/solidcraft-web/sw.js` and the small inline scripts in `apps/solidcraft-web/index.html`. Keep them minimal; `cargo xtask web-offline-test` covers the service worker.
- Python 3.11+ is allowed only for asset authoring, lint and review tools (`assets/AGENTS.md`), never as an application dependency.
- Design notes for the browser runtime: `docs/web-runtime.md`, `docs/browser-api.md`.
